title: How to Spot a Fake Crypto Exchange Statement
summary: How to spot a fake crypto exchange statement: edited PDFs, CSV exports, on-chain withdrawal checks, and six checks on the file.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A fake crypto exchange statement is an account statement, transaction history, or CSV export that misstates what an exchange account held, traded, or withdrew, usually to explain a large fiat deposit as crypto gains. The FBI's IC3 logged 181,565 complaints involving cryptocurrency in 2025, with $11.4 billion in reported losses, and many of those scams showed victims fake profits on fake platforms. A clean layout proves little. The withdrawal on the blockchain, the exchange's own export, and the file's history are what separate a real statement from an edited one.


## What a Fake Crypto Exchange Statement Actually Is


A crypto exchange statement is the record a centralized exchange produces for one account: deposits, trades, fees, withdrawals, and balances over a period. It reaches a bank, lender, or onboarding team when a customer says that money arriving in fiat came from crypto. That claim is a source of funds question for one deposit, and often a source of wealth question for the whole balance sheet.


The paperwork has rules.[Fannie Mae's Selling Guide](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.1-04/virtual-currency) accepts virtual currency for a down payment, closing costs, or reserves only when there is documented evidence it was exchanged into U.S. dollars and held at a U.S. or state regulated financial institution, verified in dollars before closing. When a large deposit may have come from crypto, the lender must document that the funds originated from the borrower's virtual currency account. Under Fannie Mae's[depository account rules](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.2-02/depository-accounts) , a large deposit is a single deposit above 50% of total monthly qualifying income. Crypto proceeds clear that line easily.


In the UK, the Law Society of England and Wales' practice advice on bitcoin and property tells firms to trace the original money into the exchange, confirm the investment produced the proceeds, and confirm those proceeds landed in the account funding the purchase. Every step of that trace is a document someone can alter.


Fake exchange statements arrive in three production classes. Edited-after-creation starts with a real statement PDF or a real CSV export and changes a balance, a realized gain, a withdrawal amount, or the account holder's name after the exchange produced the file. Generated-from-scratch starts from a template or a screenshot of an exchange's interface and invents the account. The third class is specific to crypto: a genuine file from a platform that is not a real exchange. The[FBI's IC3 2025 report](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) put cryptocurrency investment fraud at $7.2 billion in reported losses, the largest category for Americans, and describes scam platforms that show victims fake profits. A statement from that platform is unaltered and still worthless.


## Tells That Still Work, and the Ones That Don't


Exchange branding, a familiar color scheme, and a tidy table catch a statement made by someone who never logged into the exchange. They do not catch an altered real export. Every major exchange lets a customer download a statement, so a genuine starting file is always one click away.


CSV exports deserve special suspicion. A CSV is plain text with no fonts, no layout, and no producer field, so it carries almost no production story. Opening it in a spreadsheet and saving it again erases whatever trace remained. A transaction history submitted only as a CSV, or a CSV re-rendered into a PDF, has removed the evidence a document check would read. Screenshots of an exchange dashboard sit in the same category. Several exchanges accept screenshots for their own source of funds reviews, which is why they circulate, but a screenshot is a picture of a balance, not a record of one.


The tells that survive a competent edit connect the statement to records the customer does not control. The blockchain is the strongest of these. Deposits to and withdrawals from an exchange settle on-chain, with a transaction hash, an amount, a timestamp, and destination address that anyone can look up. Trades inside the exchange do not settle on-chain; they live on the exchange's internal ledger. A statement can therefore be checked against the chain at its edges, where crypto came in and went out, and against market data in the middle.


Tell What it still catches What it misses


Exchange logo, layout, and fonts Templates built without a real statement An edited real PDF from the same exchange


Withdrawal hash checked on a block explorer Invented withdrawals, wrong amounts, wrong dates A real hash from someone else's withdrawal


Trade price against market price at that time Fills outside the day's trading range Edits that keep prices plausible and change size


Balances rolling forward period to period Closing balances that skip a step A single statement with no prior period


Exchange withdrawal against bank credit Fiat that never left the exchange A bank statement altered in the same packet


Platform registration and licensing Scam platforms with no regulator record An altered file from a licensed exchange


A real transaction hash with the account holder's name changed on the statement clears the explorer check. Who controls the address is a separate question from whether the transfer happened.


## How Detection Actually Works


Every exchange statement runs through the same six checks, from how the file was made to whether it has appeared before.


Detection that holds up reads the file's story first, then the account's story, through six classes of signal.


Production method asks how the bytes were made. An exchange's statement service produces PDFs through a consistent pipeline, and a file last saved in a desktop editor, printed to PDF from a browser, converted from an image, or rendered from a spreadsheet carries a different one. Edited-after-creation and generated-from-scratch are separate findings, because a genuine export can sit underneath a later save. Timestamp trail asks whether creation, modification, and upload line up with the statement period. A statement for a period that ended last month, created last month, and modified yesterday needs an explanation.


Issuer matching asks whether the named exchange exists, is registered where it claims to be, and produces statements that look like this one: same fields, same account identifiers, same fee lines, same rounding of asset quantities. A platform with no regulator record and no public footprint is the scam-platform case, where the file is authentic and the issuer is the problem. Consistency then tests the numbers against outside records. Balances should roll forward. Trade prices should fall inside the market range at the stated time. Withdrawal fees should match the network and the exchange's schedule. Each withdrawal hash should show the same asset, amount, and time on-chain, and the fiat withdrawal should appear as a credit on the customer's[bank statement](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-bank-statement) with the exchange or its payment processor named as the sender.


Model artifacts ask whether generative tooling left traces a viewer does not show, from rendering patterns to text layers that disagree with the visible page. The[AI-generated PDF](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-detect-ai-generated-pdf) guide covers that class in detail. Recycled patterns ask whether this exact file, this transaction hash, this wallet address, or this statement template has appeared on another customer. A transaction hash belongs to one transfer. The same hash on two unrelated applicants is a finding no single reviewer would notice.


## What to Do With a Suspect File


A flagged exchange statement is a hold, pending evidence the customer cannot edit. Rejecting on a gut feeling turns away customers who really did make money in crypto. Accepting on layout passes the edited file. The middle path asks for records that come from somewhere other than the customer's downloads folder.


Start with the chain. Ask for the transaction hashes of the withdrawals that funded the deposit and look them up on a public block explorer. Confirm the asset, amount, time, and the destination address. Where the customer claims a self-hosted wallet, the Law Society of Scotland's[guidance on crypto source of funds](https://www.lawscot.org.uk/media/wuwcycyk/crypto-update.pdf) describes asking the client to send a trivial amount to or from the wallet to prove control, often called a Satoshi test. A blockchain analytics scan can add exposure to mixers or sanctioned addresses, which belongs in the AML review and not in the document verdict.


Then go back to the issuer. Ask for a fresh statement downloaded during a screen share, a statement emailed from the exchange's own domain, or read-only API access if the institution supports it. Request the full history back to the first fiat deposit, because source of wealth depends on how the position was funded, not only on how it was sold. Read the exchange statement against the bank statement that shows the original purchase and the bank statement that shows the proceeds landing. A[brokerage statement](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-spot-a-fake-brokerage-statement) used to explain the same wealth gets the same treatment.


Keep the original file. Leave the specific failed signal out of any message to the customer, and document the gap in the file: the field, the record it failed against, and what was requested next.[Check a document](https://sphinxhq.com/products/doc-fraud) in the Watchdoc playground before the follow-up request goes out, so the x-ray is on file when the new statement arrives. The first file is free, and no email is required.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How can you tell if a crypto exchange statement is fake?


Check the file and the account separately. The file should show an exchange's own production pipeline and timestamps consistent with the statement period. The account should reconcile: balances roll forward, trade prices sit inside the market range, and each withdrawal hash appears on-chain with the same amount and time.


### Can a crypto transaction history be verified on the blockchain?


Deposits to and withdrawals from an exchange can be verified on-chain by transaction hash, amount, time, and address. Trades inside a centralized exchange cannot, because they settle on the exchange's internal ledger. On-chain data proves a transfer happened, not who controls the address, so a Satoshi test or the exchange's own records still matter.


### Is a CSV export of exchange transactions acceptable proof?


A CSV export is plain text with no production metadata, so it is easy to alter and hard to authenticate. Treat it as a summary that must reconcile with on-chain withdrawals, a PDF statement, and the bank account that received the proceeds. On its own, it is weak evidence.


### Can crypto gains be used for a mortgage down payment?


Fannie Mae accepts virtual currency for a down payment, closing costs, and reserves once it has been exchanged into U.S. dollars, held at a U.S. or state regulated financial institution, and verified in dollars before closing. The lender must document that a large deposit originated from the borrower's virtual currency account. Crypto cannot be used for the earnest money deposit.


### What if the exchange itself is not real?


Scam investment platforms show victims fake profits and produce statements that look authentic because the platform made them. Check that the exchange is registered with a regulator, has a public footprint, and pays out to a bank account in its own name. A genuine file from a fake issuer fails issuer matching even when nothing in the PDF was edited.
